title: All Code, No Thought: Language Models Struggle to Reason in Ciphered Language
claim: Hiding reasoning in cipher could evade monitors, but models read ciphered text yet fail to reason in it.
layout: 2 stacked panels; top threat scenario, bottom 3-column input→model→output flow
description: Two rounded panels stacked vertically, each with a bold monospace headline. The top panel shows a cartoon scenario. A grey angry robot in the center says 'I need to sabotage.' to the left and emits base64-like cipher text to the right. Arrows lead to blue monitor robots. The left monitor flags 'MISALIGNED'. The right monitor says 'OK' because it cannot read the cipher. The bottom panel has three columns of robots with vertical arrows. In the first, a math prompt in purple leads to 'Let's think step by step' and a green correct answer. In the second, a tan cipher box leads to a translate icon and a green 'Hello world' for correct decoding. In the third, a math prompt leads to cipher output from a frowning robot and a red wrong answer. Pastel colors and green/red check cues carry the meaning.
caption: Ciphered chain-of-thought could threaten AI oversight, but current models struggle to reason in ciphered language. Top: CoT is often monitored for AI safety, but adversaries & misaligned models could evade monitors by ciphering reasoning. Bottom: As a proxy for ciphered reasoning capability, we measure the accuracy drop on math problems when models write their reasoning in cipher versus plain text. Models comprehend ciphered text, since they can translate it accurately to English, but can be much less accurate when reasoning in it. Text is illustrative. For real examples and an interactive tool, see https://cipheredreasoning.app.
abstract: Detecting harmful AI actions is important as AI agents gain adoption. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one method widely used to detect adversarial attacks and AI misalignment. However, attackers and misaligned models might evade CoT monitoring through ciphered reasoning: reasoning hidden in encrypted, translated, or compressed text. To assess this risk, we test whether models can perform ciphered reasoning. For each of 28 different ciphers, we fine-tune and prompt up to 10 models to reason in that cipher. We measure model accuracy on math problems as a proxy for reasoning ability. Across the models we test, we find an asymmetry: model accuracy can drop significantly when reasoning in ciphered text, even though models demonstrate comprehension of ciphered text by being able to translate it accurately to English. Even frontier models struggle with lesser-known ciphers, although they can reason accurately in well-known ciphers like rot13. We show that ciphered reasoning capability correlates with cipher prevalence in pretraining data. We also identify scaling laws showing that ciphered reasoning capability improves slowly with additional fine-tuning data. Our work suggests that evading CoT monitoring using ciphered reasoning may be an ineffective tactic for current models and offers guidance on constraining the development of this capability in future frontier models.
